Romania
Romania is a country in <color=#3366CC>Central</color> and Southeastern Europe. It lies on the lower course of the <color=#3366CC>Danube</color>, north of the

<color=#3366CC>Balkan Peninsula</color>, and on the northwestern shore of the <color=#3366CC>Black Sea</color>. It borders <color=#3366CC>Ukraine</color> to the north and east, <color=#3366CC>Hungary</color> to
the west, <color=#3366CC>Serbia</color> to the southwest, <color=#3366CC>Bulgaria</color> to the south, <color=#3366CC>Moldova</color> to the east, and the Black Sea to the southeast. It is
the twelfth-largest country in Europe by area, covering 238397 km2, and the sixth-most populous member state of the
European Union, with 19 million inhabitants. The capital, largest city and economic centre is <color=#3366CC>Bucharest</color>. Other major
cities include <color=#3366CC>Cluj-Napoca</color>, <color=#3366CC>Iasi</color>, <color=#3366CC>Constanta</color>, <color=#3366CC>Timisoara</color> and <color=#3366CC>Brasov</color>.
Romania was settled during the <color=#3366CC>Lower Paleolithic</color>, later becoming <color=#3366CC>Dacia</color> before Trajan's Dacian Wars and
Romanisation. The modern Romanian state was formed in 1859 with the unification of Moldavia and Wallachia under
<color=#3366CC>Alexandru Ioan Cuza</color>, becoming the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Romania</color> in 1881 under <color=#3366CC>Carol I of Romania</color>. Romania gained
independence from the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color> in 1877, formalised by the Treaty of Berlin. After <color=#3366CC>World War I</color>, <color=#3366CC>Transylvania</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Banat</color>, Bukovina, and <color=#3366CC>Bessarabia</color> joined the Old Kingdom, forming Greater Romania, which reached its largest
territorial extent. In 1940, under <color=#3366CC>Axis</color> pressure, Romania lost territories to <color=#3366CC>Hungary</color>, Bulgaria, and the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color>.
Following the Act of 23 August, Romania switched sides to join <color=#3366CC>the Allies</color>. After <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>, it regained Northern
Transylvania through the Paris Peace Treaties. Under Soviet occupation, King Michael I was forced to abdicate, and
Romania became a socialist republic and <color=#3366CC>Warsaw Pact</color> member. After the <color=#3366CC>fall of communism</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Romanian</color>
<color=#3366CC>revolution</color> in 1989, Romania transitioned to <color=#3366CC>liberal democracy</color>.
Romania is a <color=#3366CC>developed country</color> with a high-income economy and is widely regarded as a middle power in international
relations. The country possesses 11 UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Romania is a global net exporter of automotive
parts and is an increasingly prominent technology centre with some of the fastest internet speeds in the world.

Romania is a member of several <color=#3366CC>international organisations</color>, including the <color=#3366CC>European Union</color>, <color=#3366CC>NATO</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>BSEC</color>.
Etymology
Romania derives from the local name for Romanian (Romanian: român), which in turn derives from <color=#3366CC>Latin</color>, meaning
"Roman" or "of <color=#3366CC>Rome</color>". This ethnonym for Romanians is first attested in the sixteenth century by Italian humanists

travelling in <color=#3366CC>Transylvania</color>, <color=#3366CC>Moldavia</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Wallachia</color>. The oldest known surviving document written in <color=#3366CC>Romanian</color> that can
be precisely dated, a 1521 letter known as the "Letter of Neacsu from Câmpulung", is notable for including the first
documented occurrence of Romanian in a country name: Wallachia is mentioned as Tara Rumânească.
History
Prehistory
Human remains found in Pestera cu Oase ("Cave with Bones"), radiocarbon date from circa 40,000 years ago, and
represent the oldest known <color=#3366CC>Homo sapiens</color> in Europe. <color=#3366CC>Neolithic</color> agriculture spread after the arrival of a mixed group of
people from <color=#3366CC>Thessaly</color> in the 6th millennium BC. Excavations at the Poiana Slatinei site near a salt spring next to Lunca,
Neamt yielded the earliest evidence for salt exploitation in Europe; here salt production began between the 5th and 4th
millennium BC. The first permanent settlements developed into "proto-cities", which were larger than 800 acre. The
<color=#3366CC>Cucuteni–Trypillia culture</color>—the best known <color=#3366CC>archaeological culture</color> of Old Europe—flourished in Muntenia, southeastern
Transylvania and northeastern Moldavia in the 3rd millennium BC. The first fortified settlements appeared around 1800
BC, showing the militant character of <color=#3366CC>Bronze Age</color> societies.
Antiquity
Greek colonies established on the <color=#3366CC>Black Sea</color> coast in the 7th century BC became important centres of commerce with
the local tribes. Among the native peoples, <color=#3366CC>Herodotus</color> listed the Getae of the Lower Danube region, the Agathyrsi of
Transylvania and the Syginnae of the plains along the river Tisza at the beginning of the 5th century BC. Centuries
later, <color=#3366CC>Strabo</color> associated the Getae with the <color=#3366CC>Dacians</color> who dominated the lands along the southern <color=#3366CC>Carpathian Mountains</color>
in the 1st century BC. <color=#3366CC>Burebista</color> was the first Dacian ruler to unite the local tribes. He also conquered the Greek
colonies in <color=#3366CC>Dobruja</color> and the neighbouring peoples as far as the Middle Danube and the <color=#3366CC>Balkan Mountains</color> between
around 55 and 44 BC. After Burebista was murdered in 44 BC, his kingdom collapsed.
The Romans reached <color=#3366CC>Dacia</color> during Burebista's reign and conquered Dobruja in 46 AD. Dacia was again united under
<color=#3366CC>Decebalus</color> around 85 AD. He resisted the Romans for decades, but the Roman army defeated his troops in 106 AD.
Emperor <color=#3366CC>Trajan</color> transformed <color=#3366CC>Banat</color>, Oltenia and the greater part of Transylvania into a new province called Roman
Dacia, but Dacian, <color=#3366CC>Germanic</color> and <color=#3366CC>Sarmatian</color> tribes continued to dominate the lands along the Roman frontiers. The
Romans pursued an organised colonisation policy, and the provincials enjoyed a long period of peace and prosperity in
the 2nd century. Scholars accepting the Daco-Roman continuity theory—one of the main theories about the origin of
the Romanians—say that the cohabitation of the native <color=#3366CC>Dacians</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Roman</color> colonists in Roman Dacia was the first
phase of the Romanians' ethnogenesis. The Carpians, <color=#3366CC>Goths</color> and other neighbouring tribes made regular raids against
Dacia from the 210s. The Romans could not resist, and Emperor <color=#3366CC>Aurelian</color> ordered the evacuation of the province Dacia
Trajana in the 270s. Scholars supporting the continuity theory are convinced that most Latin-speaking commoners
stayed behind when the army and civil administration was withdrawn. The Romans did not abandon their fortresses
along the northern banks of the <color=#3366CC>Lower Danube</color> for decades, and <color=#3366CC>Dobruja</color> (known as Scythia Minor) remained an
integral part of the Roman Empire until the early 7th century.
Middle Ages
The Goths were expanding towards the Lower Danube from the 230s, forcing the native peoples to flee to the <color=#3366CC>Roman</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color> or to accept their <color=#3366CC>suzerainty</color>. The Goths' rule ended abruptly when the <color=#3366CC>Huns</color> invaded their territory in 376,
causing new waves of migrations. The Huns forced the remnants of the local population into submission, but their
empire collapsed in 454. The Gepids took possession of the former Dacia province. Place names that are of <color=#3366CC>Slavic</color>
origin abound in Romania, indicating that a significant Slavic-speaking population lived in the territory. The first <color=#3366CC>Slavic</color>
groups settled in <color=#3366CC>Moldavia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Wallachia</color> in the 6th century, in Transylvania around 600. The nomadic <color=#3366CC>Avars</color> defeated
the Gepids and established a powerful empire around 570. The <color=#3366CC>Bulgars</color>, who also came from the European Pontic
steppe, occupied the <color=#3366CC>Lower Danube</color> region in 680.
After the <color=#3366CC>Avar Khaganate</color> collapsed in the 790s, the <color=#3366CC>First Bulgarian Empire</color> became the dominant power of the region,
occupying lands as far as the river Tisa. The <color=#3366CC>First Bulgarian Empire</color> had a mixed population consisting of the <color=#3366CC>Bulgar</color>
conquerors, <color=#3366CC>Slavs</color> and Vlachs (or Romanians) but the Slavicisation of the Bulgar elite had already begun in the 9th
century. Following the conquest of southern <color=#3366CC>Transylvania</color> around 830, people from the Bulgar Empire mined salt at the
local salt mines. The Council of Preslav declared <color=#3366CC>Old Church Slavonic</color> the language of liturgy in the country in 893. The
Vlachs also adopted Old Church Slavonic as their liturgical language.
The Magyars (or Hungarians) took control of the steppes north of the Lower Danube in the 830s, but the Bulgarians
and the <color=#3366CC>Pechenegs</color> forced them to abandon this region for the <color=#3366CC>lowlands along the Middle Danube</color> around 894.
Centuries later, the Gesta Hungarorum wrote of the invading Magyars' wars against three dukes—Glad, Menumorut
and the Vlach Gelou—for <color=#3366CC>Banat</color>, Crisana and <color=#3366CC>Transylvania</color>. The Gesta also listed many peoples—<color=#3366CC>Slavs</color>, Bulgarians,
Vlachs, <color=#3366CC>Khazars</color>, and Székelys—inhabiting the same regions. The reliability of the Gesta is debated. Some scholars
regard it as a basically accurate account, others describe it as a literary work filled with invented details. The
Pechenegs seized the lowlands abandoned by the Hungarians to the east of the <color=#3366CC>Carpathians</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Byzantine</color> missionaries proselytised in the lands east of the Tisa from the 940s and <color=#3366CC>Byzantine</color> troops occupied <color=#3366CC>Dobruja</color>
in the 970s. The first king of Hungary, <color=#3366CC>Stephen I</color>, who supported <color=#3366CC>Western European</color> missionaries, defeated the local
chieftains and established Roman Catholic bishoprics (office of a bishop) in <color=#3366CC>Transylvania</color> and <color=#3366CC>Banat</color> in the early 11th
century. Significant Pecheneg groups fled to the Byzantine Empire in the 1040s; the Oghuz Turks followed them, and
the nomadic <color=#3366CC>Cumans</color> became the dominant power of the steppes in the 1060s. Cooperation between the Cumans and
the Vlachs against the Byzantine Empire is well documented from the end of the 11th century. Scholars who reject the
Daco-Roman continuity theory say that the first Vlach groups left their <color=#3366CC>Balkan</color> homeland for the mountain pastures of
the eastern and southern Carpathians in the 11th century, establishing the Romanians' presence in the lands to the
north of the Lower Danube.
Exposed to nomadic incursions, Transylvania developed into an important border province of the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Hungary</color>.
The Székelys—a community of free warriors—settled in <color=#3366CC>central Transylvania</color> around 1100 and moved to the
easternmost regions around 1200. Colonists from the <color=#3366CC>Holy Roman Empire</color>—the Transylvanian Saxons'
ancestors—came to the province in the 1150s. A high-ranking royal official, styled voivode, ruled the Transylvanian
counties from the 1170s, but the <color=#3366CC>Székely</color> and <color=#3366CC>Saxon</color> seats (or districts) were not subject to the voivodes' authority.
Royal charters wrote of the "Vlachs' land" in southern Transylvania in the early 13th century, indicating the existence of
autonomous Romanian communities. Papal correspondence mentions the activities of Orthodox prelates among the
Romanians in Muntenia in the 1230s. Also in the 13th century, the <color=#3366CC>Republic of Genoa</color> started establishing <color=#3366CC>colonies</color> on
the <color=#3366CC>Black Sea</color>, including Calafat, and <color=#3366CC>Constanta</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>Mongols</color> destroyed large territories during <color=#3366CC>their invasion of Eastern and Central Europe</color> in 1241 and 1242. The
Mongols' <color=#3366CC>Golden Horde</color> emerged as the dominant power of Eastern Europe, but <color=#3366CC>Béla IV</color> of <color=#3366CC>Hungary</color>'s land grant to the
<color=#3366CC>Knights Hospitallers</color> in Oltenia and Muntenia shows that the local Vlach rulers were subject to the king's authority in
1247. Basarab I of Wallachia united the Romanian polities between the southern <color=#3366CC>Carpathians</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Lower Danube</color> in
the 1310s. He defeated the Hungarian royal army in the Battle of Posada and secured the independence of <color=#3366CC>Wallachia</color>
in 1330. The second Romanian principality, <color=#3366CC>Moldavia</color>, achieved full autonomy during the reign of Bogdan I around
1360. A local dynasty ruled the Despotate of Dobruja in the second half of the 14th century, but the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color>
took possession of the territory after 1388.
Princes <color=#3366CC>Mircea I</color> and <color=#3366CC>Vlad III of Wallachia</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Stephen III of Moldavia</color> defended their countries' independence against
the Ottomans. Most <color=#3366CC>Wallachian</color> and Moldavian princes paid a regular tribute to the Ottoman sultans from 1417 and
1456, respectively. <color=#3366CC>John Hunyadi</color>, organised the defence of the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Hungary</color> and anti-Ottoman campaigns from
1440 until his death in 1456. Increasing taxes outraged the Transylvanian peasants, and they rose up in an open
rebellion in 1437, but the Hungarian nobles and the heads of the <color=#3366CC>Saxon</color> and <color=#3366CC>Székely</color> communities jointly suppressed
their revolt. The formal alliance of the Hungarian, Saxon, and Székely leaders, known as the Union of the Three
Nations, became an important element of the self-government of <color=#3366CC>Transylvania</color>. The Orthodox Romanian knezes
("chiefs") were excluded from the Union.
Early modern times and national awakening
The <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Hungary</color> collapsed, and the Ottomans occupied parts of <color=#3366CC>Banat</color> and Crisana in 1541. Transylvania and
Maramures, along with the rest of Banat and Crisana, developed into a new state under Ottoman suzerainty, the
Principality of Transylvania. The <color=#3366CC>Reformation</color>, initiated in <color=#3366CC>Germany</color> by <color=#3366CC>Martin Luther</color> in 1517, encouraged the spread of
<color=#3366CC>Protestantism</color> across the region; by 1568, the Edict of Torda formally granted local communities the right to choose
their own preachers, sanctioning the existence of four "received" religions (<color=#3366CC>Catholicism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Lutheranism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Calvinism</color>, and
Unitarianism). The Romanians' Orthodox faith remained only tolerated, although they made up more than one-third of
the population, according to 17th-century estimates. In June 1609, Gabriel Báthory freed the Romanian Orthodox
clergy from both taxation and service demands.

The princes of <color=#3366CC>Transylvania</color>, <color=#3366CC>Wallachia</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Moldavia</color> joined the Holy League against the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color> in 1594. The
Wallachian prince, <color=#3366CC>Michael the Brave</color>, united the three principalities under his rule in May 1600. The neighbouring
powers forced him to abdicate in September, but he became a symbol of the unification of the Romanian lands in the
19th century. Although the rulers of the three principalities continued to pay tribute to the Ottomans, the most talented
princes—Gabriel Bethlen of Transylvania, Matei Basarab of Wallachia, and Vasile Lupu of Moldavia—strengthened
their autonomy.
The united armies of the Holy League expelled the Ottoman troops from <color=#3366CC>Central Europe</color> between 1684 and 1699, and
the Principality of Transylvania was integrated into the <color=#3366CC>Habsburg monarchy</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Habsburgs</color> supported the Catholic
clergy and persuaded the Orthodox Romanian prelates to accept the union with the Roman Catholic Church in 1699. In
the 18th century, <color=#3366CC>Moldavia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Wallachia</color> maintained their internal autonomy, but in 1711 and 1716, respectively, the
period of the Phanariots began, with rulers appointed directly by the Porte from among the noble families of Greek
origin in <color=#3366CC>Constantinople</color>. With the signing of the Ausgleich in 1867, <color=#3366CC>Transylvania</color> quickly lost its remaining political
autonomy, being politically and administratively incorporated into the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Hungary</color>. The Church Union
strengthened the Romanian intellectuals' devotion to their Roman heritage. The Orthodox Church was restored in
Transylvania only after Orthodox monks stirred up revolts in 1744 and 1759. The organisation of the Transylvanian
Military Frontier caused further disturbances, especially among the Székelys in 1764.
Princes Dimitrie Cantemir of Moldavia and Constantin Brâncoveanu of <color=#3366CC>Wallachia</color> concluded alliances with the
<color=#3366CC>Habsburg Monarchy</color> and <color=#3366CC>Russia</color> against the Ottomans, but they were dethroned in 1711 and 1714, respectively. The
sultans lost confidence in the native princes and appointed Orthodox merchants from the Phanar district of <color=#3366CC>Istanbul</color> to
rule <color=#3366CC>Moldavia</color> and Wallachia. The Phanariot princes pursued oppressive fiscal policies and dissolved the army. The
neighbouring powers took advantage of the situation: the Habsburg Monarchy annexed the northwestern part of
Moldavia, or Bukovina, in 1775, and the <color=#3366CC>Russian Empire</color> seized the eastern half of Moldavia, or <color=#3366CC>Bessarabia</color>, in 1812.
A census revealed that the Romanians were more numerous than any other ethnic group in <color=#3366CC>Transylvania</color> in 1733, but
legislation continued to use contemptuous adjectives (such as "tolerated" and "admitted") when referring to them. The
Uniate bishop, Inocentiu Micu-Klein, who demanded recognition of the Romanians as the fourth privileged nation, was
forced into exile. Uniate and Orthodox clerics and laymen jointly signed a plea for the Transylvanian Romanians'
emancipation in 1791, but the monarch and the local authorities refused to grant their requests.
The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca authorised the Russian ambassador in <color=#3366CC>Istanbul</color> to defend the autonomy of Moldavia and
Wallachia (known as the Danubian Principalities) in 1774. Taking advantage of the <color=#3366CC>Greek War of Independence</color>, a
Wallachian lesser nobleman, Tudor Vladimirescu, stirred up a revolt against the Ottomans in January 1821, but he was
murdered in June by Phanariot Greeks. After a new Russo-Turkish War, the Treaty of Adrianople strengthened the
autonomy of the Danubian Principalities in 1829, although it also acknowledged the sultan's right to confirm the election
of the princes.
Mihail Kogălniceanu, Nicolae Bălcescu and other leaders of the 1848 revolutions in Moldavia and Wallachia demanded
the emancipation of the peasants and the union of the two principalities, but Russian and Ottoman troops crushed their
revolt. The Wallachian revolutionaries were the first to adopt the blue, yellow and red tricolour as the national flag,
which included the motto "Justice, Fraternity" (Dreptate, Frătie) to symbolise the bond between Wallachians and
Moldavians. In Transylvania, most Romanians supported the imperial government against the <color=#3366CC>Hungarian</color>
<color=#3366CC>revolutionaries</color> after the Diet passed a law concerning the union of <color=#3366CC>Transylvania</color> and <color=#3366CC>Hungary</color>. Bishop Andrei Saguna
proposed the unification of the Romanians of the Habsburg Monarchy in a separate duchy, but the central government
refused to change the internal borders.
Unification and the Kingdom of Romania
From the Little Union to the Great War
The modern Romanian state was created through the unification of the principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia,
accepted as a federative structure by the Great Powers following the Paris Convention of 1858, and later cemented by
the simultaneous election as ruler of both states of the unionist <color=#3366CC>Alexandru Ioan Cuza</color>. After carrying out numerous
reforms that laid the foundations for the modernisation of the state, he was forced in 1866 by a broad coalition of the
political parties of the time, also known as the "Monstrous coalition", to abdicate and leave the country.
The union was at one time in peril, but the political leaders of the era succeeded in placing on the princely throne <color=#3366CC>Carol</color>
<color=#3366CC>I of Romania</color>, who accepted the Constitution and took the oath on 10 May 1866. Eleven years later, on 10 May 1877,
Romania proclaimed its independence—achieved on the battlefield—and in 1881, on the same day of the year, Carol
was crowned as King of Romania. In 1913, Romania entered the <color=#3366CC>Second Balkan War</color> against <color=#3366CC>Bulgaria</color>, at the end of
which it obtained Southern Dobruja. In 1914, <color=#3366CC>King Carol I</color> died, and his nephew, Ferdinand I, succeeded him on the
throne.
World War I and the Great Union
In 1916, Romania entered <color=#3366CC>World War I</color> on the side of the <color=#3366CC>Entente Powers</color>. Although the Romanian forces did not
perform well militarily, by the end of the war the <color=#3366CC>Austrian</color> and <color=#3366CC>Russian Empires</color> had disintegrated; the National
Assembly in <color=#3366CC>Transylvania</color>, and the Sfatul Tării in <color=#3366CC>Bessarabia</color> and Bukovina proclaimed their union with Romania, and
King Ferdinand I and Queen Maria were crowned sovereign of all Romanians in Alba Iulia on 15 October 1922.
After <color=#3366CC>World War I</color>, the union of Bukovina with Romania was ratified in 1919 by the Treaty of Saint Germain. Most of the
territories claimed by Romania from the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Hungary</color>—Crisana, <color=#3366CC>Transylvania</color> and parts of <color=#3366CC>Banat</color> and
Maramures—were annexed to the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Romania</color>. This act was ratified in 1920 by the <color=#3366CC>Treaty of Trianon</color>, which
defined the new border between <color=#3366CC>Hungary</color> and Romania.
Interwar period
After having left the country and renounced his claim to the throne in 1925, Carol II returned in 1930 and usurped his
son's throne; influenced by his inner circle—referred to by historians as the "Royal Camarilla"—he gradually
undermined the democratic system, and in 1938 he assumed dictatorial powers. Although he was pro-Western
(especially Anglophile), Carol attempted to appease extreme centrifugal forces by appointing nationalist governments
that adopted anti-Semitic measures, such as the Goga cabinet and the one led by the Orthodox Patriarch Miron
Cristea.
World War II
Following the <color=#3366CC>Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact</color> of 1939, in June 1940 Romania accepted the loss of <color=#3366CC>Bessarabia</color>, Northern
Bukovina and the Hertsa region in favour of the <color=#3366CC>USSR</color> (as stipulated in the Soviet ultimatum of 28 June 1940).
Unaware of the details of the Soviet–German pact, Carol attempted to secure an alliance with <color=#3366CC>Nazi Germany</color>, and
appointed Ion Gigurtu as President of the Council of Ministers, who declared that he would pursue a <color=#3366CC>Nazi</color> pro-Axis
(<color=#3366CC>Berlin</color>–<color=#3366CC>Rome</color>) policy that was anti-Semitic and fascist-totalitarian in nature. Between 4 July and 4 September 1940, by
accepting Hitler's arbitration over <color=#3366CC>Transylvania</color> (after Gigurtu declared on radio that Romania must make territorial
sacrifices to justify its Nazi orientation and full adherence to the Berlin–Rome Axis), Romania ceded Northern
Transylvania—including the city of <color=#3366CC>Cluj</color>—to Hungary. The vast territories in Transylvania ceded by Ion Gigurtu to
Hungary contained important natural resources, including gold mines. Ion Gigurtu also initiated negotiations to cede
8,000 km2 of Southern Dobruja to <color=#3366CC>Bulgaria</color>, these negotiations were interrupted by Antonescu's unconditional
acceptance of the territorial cession.
In response to the chaotic withdrawal from <color=#3366CC>Bessarabia</color>, the territorial cessions, public discontent, and protests from
political leaders, King Carol II suspended the 1938 Constitution of Romania and appointed General <color=#3366CC>Ion Antonescu</color> as
Prime Minister. This measure, supported by the Iron Guard, demanded that the king abdicate in favour of his son,
Mihai. Subsequently, Antonescu assumed dictatorial powers and became President of the Council of Ministers, as the
self-titled "Leader" of the state.
In 1941, as an ally of <color=#3366CC>Nazi Germany</color>, Romania entered <color=#3366CC>World War II</color> by declaring war on the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color>. A shift in
fortunes only became discernible after the defeat at <color=#3366CC>Stalingrad</color> and the subsequent change of the USSR from a
defensive to an offensive posture. On 23 August 1944, with the Soviet army having been present in northern Moldova
since March, King Mihai I forcibly removed Marshal <color=#3366CC>Ion Antonescu</color> from power, as he refused to sign an armistice with
the <color=#3366CC>Allies of World War II</color>. Following Antonescu's outright refusal, King Mihai I ordered the dismissal and arrest of the
marshal, and Romania switched sides to join the Allies.
Socialist Romania (1947–1989)
Less than three years after the Soviet occupation of Romania, in 1947, King Michael I was forced to abdicate and the
People's Republic of Romania—a state of "popular democracy"—was proclaimed. The newly established communist
regime, led by the Romanian Workers' Party, consolidated its power through a Stalinist-type policy aimed at
suppressing any political opposition and transforming the economic and social structures of the old bourgeois regime.
In the early 1960s, the Romanian government began asserting a certain degree of independence from the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color>
in its foreign policy, although it did not abandon its repressive policies (which it labelled "revolutionary conquests") in
domestic affairs. In 1965, communist leader Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej died, ushering in a period of change in Romania.
After a brief power struggle, <color=#3366CC>Nicolae Ceausescu</color> emerged as the head of the communist party, becoming General
Secretary of the Romanian Communist Party in 1965, President of the State Council in 1967, and President of the
Socialist Republic of Romania in 1974. Ceausescu's rule from 1965 to 1989 grew increasingly authoritarian during the
Romania since 1989
In the context of the fall of communism throughout <color=#3366CC>Eastern Europe</color> during the <color=#3366CC>revolutions of 1989</color>, a protest in support
of Reformed pastor László Tőkés that began in December 1989 in <color=#3366CC>Timisoara</color> quickly escalated into a national uprising
against the communist regime, ultimately resulting in the execution of Ceausescu and his wife Elena on 25 December
An interim council composed of figures from civil society and former communist officials assumed control of the
government, and <color=#3366CC>Ion Iliescu</color> became the provisional president of the country. The new government reversed many of
the authoritarian communist policies and dismissed several leaders of the former regime, although still influenced by
members of the former regime (the basis for the Golaniad, and Mineriads).
In May 1990, the first free elections in Romania since the 1937 elections were held, with Iliescu of the National
Salvation Front winning the presidency with 85% of the vote. In 1992, he was reelected in the first election after the
adoption of a permanent constitution via a referendum held the previous year. <color=#3366CC>Illiescu</color> lost the 1996 election to Emil
Constantinescu, but returned to power in 2000. Traian Băsescu was elected president in 2004 and 2009, serving until
2014 at which point Klaus Iohannis succeeded him, being re-elected in 2019 and serving until 2025. During these years
several events occurred. In 2009, the country was bailed out by the <color=#3366CC>International Monetary Fund</color> as result of the Great
Recession in Europe following the <color=#3366CC>2008 financial crisis</color>.
The post-1989 period has been characterised by the privatisation and closure of several former industrial and economic
enterprises from the communist period, while corruption has been a major issue in contemporary politics.
A National Anticorruption Directorate was formed in the country in 2002. During the 2000s, Romania had one of the
highest economic growth rates in <color=#3366CC>Europe</color> and has been referred at times as "the Tiger of Eastern Europe". This has
been accompanied by a significant improvement in living standards as the country successfully reduced domestic
<color=#3366CC>poverty</color> and established a functional democratic state. However, Romania's development suffered a major setback
during the <color=#3366CC>late 2000s' recession</color> leading to a large <color=#3366CC>gross domestic product</color> contraction and a budget deficit in 2009. This
led to Romania borrowing from the <color=#3366CC>International Monetary Fund</color>. Worsening economic conditions led to unrest and
triggered a political crisis in 2012.
Since 2014, Romania launched an anti-corruption effort that led to the prosecution of medium- and high-level political,
judicial and administrative offences by the National Anticorruption Directorate. In 2015, massive anti-corruption protests
which developed in the wake of the Colectiv nightclub fire led to the resignation of prime minister Victor Ponta. During
2017–2019, in response to measures which were perceived to weaken the fight against <color=#3366CC>corruption</color>, some of the biggest
post-1989 protests took place in Romania, with over 500,000 people protesting nationwide.
The 2021 Romanian political crisis led to the ousting of Florin Cîtu's incumbent government. The Ciucă Cabinet then
took power, with Romania since having experienced a shift towards authoritarianism and <color=#3366CC>illiberalism</color>, as well as an
increased corruption. Around this time, Romania was also hit by the COVID-19 pandemic. In the 2024 presidential
election, Independent candidate Călin Georgescu achieved a surprise win in the first round. However, the
Constitutional Court annulled the election results, citing Russian meddling. The cancellation led to far-right protests,
criticism by the Trump administration, and Ilie Bolojan becoming acting president in February 2025 as Iohannis
resigned to political pressure. In the subsequent 2025 Romanian presidential election, Bucharest Mayor Nicusor Dan
was elected president.
Geography
Romania is the largest country in Southeastern Europe and the twelfth-largest in <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>, having an area of 238397
km2. It lies between latitudes 43° and 49° N and longitudes 20° and 30° E. The terrain is distributed roughly equally

between <color=#3366CC>mountains</color>, <color=#3366CC>hills</color>, and <color=#3366CC>plains</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Carpathian Mountains</color> dominate the centre of Romania, with 14 mountain
ranges reaching above 2000 m—the highest is Moldoveanu Peak at 2544 m. They are surrounded by the Moldavian
and Transylvanian plateaus, the Pannonian Plain and the Wallachian plains.
Romania is home to six terrestrial ecoregions: Balkan mixed forests, Central European mixed forests, East European
forest steppe, Pannonian mixed forests, Carpathian montane conifer forests, and Pontic steppe. Natural and
semi-natural ecosystems cover about 47% of the country's land area. There are almost 10000 km2 (about 5% of the
total area) of protected areas in Romania covering 13 <color=#3366CC>national parks</color> and three <color=#3366CC>biosphere</color> reserves. The <color=#3366CC>Danube</color> river
forms a large part of the border with <color=#3366CC>Serbia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Bulgaria</color>, and flows into the <color=#3366CC>Black Sea</color>, forming the Danube Delta,
which is the second-largest and best-preserved delta in Europe, and a <color=#3366CC>biosphere reserve</color> and a biodiversity <color=#3366CC>World</color>
<color=#3366CC>Heritage Site</color>. At 5800 km2, the Danube Delta is the largest continuous marshland in <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>, and supports 1,688
different plant species alone.
Romania has one of the largest areas of undisturbed forest in Europe, covering almost 27% of its territory. The country
had a 2019 Forest Landscape Integrity Index mean score of 5.95/10, ranking it 90th globally out of 172 countries. Some
3,700 plant species have been identified in the country, from which to date 23 have been declared natural monuments,
74 extinct, 39 endangered, 171 vulnerable, and 1,253 rare.
The fauna of Romania consists of 33,792 species of animals, 33,085 <color=#3366CC>invertebrate</color> and 707 <color=#3366CC>vertebrate</color>, with almost 400

unique species of <color=#3366CC>mammals</color>, <color=#3366CC>birds</color>, <color=#3366CC>reptiles</color>, and <color=#3366CC>amphibians</color>, including about 50% of Europe's (excluding Russia)
<color=#3366CC>brown bears</color> and 20% of its <color=#3366CC>wolves</color>.
Romania is often seen by most as having the shape resembling one of a goldfish.
Climate
Owing to its distance from open sea and its position on the southeastern portion of the European continent, Romania
has a climate that is <color=#3366CC>continental</color>, with four distinct seasons. The average annual temperature is 11 °C in the south and 8
°C in the north. In summer, average maximum temperatures in Bucharest rise to 28 °C, and temperatures over 35 °C
are fairly common in the lower-lying areas of the country. In winter, the average maximum temperature is below 2 °C.
Precipitation is average, with over 750 mm per year only on the highest western mountains, while around Bucharest it
drops to approximately 570 mm. There are some regional differences: in western sections, such as <color=#3366CC>Banat</color>, the climate
is milder and has some Mediterranean influences; the eastern part of the country has a more pronounced continental
climate. In <color=#3366CC>Dobruja</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Black Sea</color> also exerts an influence over the region's climate.
Government and politics
Romania is a <color=#3366CC>unitary</color> <color=#3366CC>semi-presidential</color> <color=#3366CC>representative democratic</color> republic with a structured system of governance and
an active civil society. The President, elected by popular vote, serves as the <color=#3366CC>head of state</color>, representing the country in
international affairs, safeguarding constitutional order, and acting as <color=#3366CC>supreme commander</color> of the Romanian Armed
Forces. The Prime Minister, appointed by the President and confirmed by the Parliament, acts as the <color=#3366CC>head of</color>
<color=#3366CC>government</color>, responsible for overseeing the executive branch, implementing domestic and foreign policies, and
managing <color=#3366CC>public administration</color>. <color=#3366CC>Legislative authority</color> is vested in a <color=#3366CC>bicameral</color> Parliament, consisting of the Chamber of
Deputies and the Senate, whose members are elected through a proportional representation system. The judiciary
operates <color=#3366CC>independently</color>, with the High Court of Cassation and Justice as the highest court of appeal.
According to International IDEA's Global State of Democracy (GSoD) Indices and Democracy Tracker, Romania
performs in the mid- range on overall democratic measures, with particular strengths in inclusive suffrage and elected
government.
Government
Romania has a democratic, multi-party system, with <color=#3366CC>legislative power</color> vested in the government and the <color=#3366CC>two chambers</color>
of the Parliament, more specifically the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate. The <color=#3366CC>judiciary</color> is <color=#3366CC>independent</color> of the
executive and the legislature. The latter is elected by popular vote for a maximum of two terms of five years and
appoints the prime minister who in turn appoints the Council of Ministers. The legislative branch of the government,
collectively known as the Parliament (residing at the Palace of the Parliament), consists of two chambers (Senate and
Chamber of Deputies) whose members are elected every four years by simple plurality.
The justice system is independent of the other branches of government and is made up of a hierarchical system of
courts with the High Court of Cassation and Justice being the supreme court of Romania. There are also courts of
appeal, county courts and local courts. The Romanian judicial system is strongly influenced by the <color=#3366CC>French model</color>, is
based on <color=#3366CC>civil law</color> and is inquisitorial in nature. The Constitutional Court (Curtea Constitutională) is responsible for
judging the compliance of laws and other state regulations with the constitution, which is the fundamental law of the
country and can be amended only through a <color=#3366CC>public referendum</color>. Romania's 2007 entry into the EU has been a
significant influence on its domestic policy, and including judicial reforms, increased judicial cooperation with other
member states, and measures to combat corruption. The Economist Intelligence Unit rated Romania as a "flawed
democracy" in 2025.
Administrative divisions
Romania is divided into 41 counties (judete) and the municipality of <color=#3366CC>Bucharest</color>. Each county is administered by a
county council, responsible for local affairs, as well as a prefect responsible for the administration of national affairs at
the county level. The prefect is appointed by the central government but cannot be a member of any political party.
Each county is subdivided further into cities and communes, which have their own mayor and local council. There are a
total of 320 cities and 2,861 communes in Romania. A total of 103 of the larger cities have municipality status, which
gives them greater administrative power over local affairs. The municipality of Bucharest is a special case, as it enjoys
a status on par to that of a county. It is further divided into six sectors and has a prefect, a general mayor (primar
general), and a general city council.
The NUTS-3 (Nomenclature of Territorial Units for Statistics) level divisions of the EU reflect Romania's
administrative-territorial structure and correspond to the 41 counties plus Bucharest. The cities and communes
correspond to the NUTS-5 level divisions, but there are no current NUTS-4 level divisions. The NUTS-1 (four
macroregions) and NUTS-2 (eight development regions) divisions exist but have no administrative capacity and are
used instead for coordinating regional development projects and statistical purposes.
Foreign relations
Since December 1989, Romania has pursued a policy of strengthening relations with the West in general, more
specifically with the <color=#3366CC>United States</color> and the <color=#3366CC>EU</color>, albeit with limited relations involving the <color=#3366CC>Russian Federation</color>. It joined
<color=#3366CC>NATO</color> on 29 March 2004, the EU on 1 January 2007, while it joined the <color=#3366CC>International Monetary Fund</color> and the <color=#3366CC>World</color>
<color=#3366CC>Bank</color> in 1972, and is a founding member of the <color=#3366CC>World Trade Organization</color>. Romania is recognised as a middle power
for its military capabilities, as well as its active diplomatic engagement on the global stage.
Recent governments have stated that their goals include strengthening ties with and helping other countries (in
particular <color=#3366CC>Moldova</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ukraine</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Georgia</color>) with better integration with the rest of the West. Romania has also made
clear since the late 1990s that it supports NATO and EU membership for the democratic former Soviet republics in
<color=#3366CC>Eastern Europe</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Caucasus</color>.
Romania applied to join to the <color=#3366CC>Schengen Area</color> in 2007, acquiring full membership in 2025 along with Bulgaria. In
December 2005, President Traian Băsescu and United States Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice signed an
agreement that would allow a U.S. military presence at several Romanian facilities primarily in the eastern part of the
country. In 2009, US Secretary of State <color=#3366CC>Hillary Clinton</color> referred to Romania as "one of the most trustworthy and
respectable US allies". However, by 2025, relations had worsened, with US vice president JD Vance in February
scolding "flimsy suspicions" and "enormous pressure from its continental neighbours" for causing the annulment of the
2024 Romanian presidential election in which Călin Georgescu won the first round.
Relations with Moldova are a special case given that the two countries share the same language and a <color=#3366CC>common</color>
<color=#3366CC>history</color>. A movement for unification of Moldova and Romania appeared in the early 1990s after both countries achieved
emancipation from communist rule but lost ground in the mid-1990s when a new Moldovan government pursued an
agenda towards preserving a Moldovan republic independent of Romania. After the 2009 protests in Moldova and the
subsequent removal of Communists from power, relations between the two countries have improved considerably.
Military
The Romanian Armed Forces consist of land, air, and naval forces led by a Commander-in-chief under the supervision
of the Ministry of National Defence, and by the president as the Supreme Commander during wartime. The Armed
Forces consist of approximately 55,000 reservists and 71,500 active military personnel—35,800 for land, 10,700 for air,
6,600 for naval forces, and 16,500 in other fields. Total defence spending in 2023 accounted for 2.44% of total national
GDP, or approximately US$8.48 billion, with a total of $9 billion intended to be spent until 2026 for modernisation and
acquisition of new equipment. Conscription stopped in 2007, when Romania switched to a volunteer army.
The Air Force operates F-16AM/BM MLU fighters, C-27J Spartan and <color=#3366CC>C-130 Hercules</color> <color=#3366CC>transport aircraft</color>, as well as IAR
330 and IAR 316 helicopters. A procurement programme for <color=#3366CC>F-35</color> fifth-generation fighters is also currently being carried
out. The Naval Forces operate three frigates, of which two are Type 22 frigates acquired from the British <color=#3366CC>Royal Navy</color>,
as well as four corvettes. The River Flotilla operates Mihail Kogălniceanu and Smârdan-class river monitors.
Romania contributed troops to the international coalition in <color=#3366CC>Afghanistan</color> beginning in 2002, with a peak deployment of
1,600 troops in 2010 (which was the 4th largest contribution according to the US). Its combat mission in the country
concluded in 2014. Romanian troops participated in the occupation of Iraq, reaching a peak of 730 soldiers before
being slowly drawn down to 350 soldiers. Romania terminated its mission in <color=#3366CC>Iraq</color> and withdrew its last troops on 24 July
2009, among the last countries to do so. The frigate the Regele Ferdinand participated in the 2011 military intervention
in Libya.
In December 2011, the Romanian Senate unanimously adopted the draft law ratifying the Romania-United States
agreement signed in September of the same year that would allow the establishment and operation of a US land-based
ballistic missile defence system in Romania as part of NATO's efforts to build a continental missile shield. The Aegis
Ashore missile system based at Deveslu became operational in 2016.
In 2024, construction work started on expanding the Mihail Kogălniceanu Air Base (RoAF 57th Air Base). The air base
is set to become the largest <color=#3366CC>NATO</color> base in <color=#3366CC>Europe</color> after the implementation of a project spanning 20 years.
Economy
In 2024, Romania had a <color=#3366CC>GDP</color> (PPP) of around $894 billion and a GDP per capita (<color=#3366CC>PPP</color>) of $47,203. According to the
<color=#3366CC>World Bank</color>, Romania is a high-income economy. According to Eurostat, Romania's GDP per capita (PPS) was 77% of
the EU average (100%) in 2022, an increase from 44% in 2007 (the year of Romania's accession to the EU), making
Romania one of the fastest growing economies in the <color=#3366CC>EU</color>.
The Bucharest Stock Exchange (BVB) is the <color=#3366CC>stock exchange</color> of Romania, located in <color=#3366CC>Bucharest</color>. In 2024, the BVB
boasted a $74 billion <color=#3366CC>market capitalisation</color> and a trading volume of $7.2 billion. As of 2024, 86 companies were listed
on the exchange. In September 2020, FTSE Russell upgraded the BVB from a Frontier market to a Secondary
Emerging Market.
After 1989 the country experienced a decade of economic instability and decline, led in part by an obsolete <color=#3366CC>industrial</color>
<color=#3366CC>base</color> and a lack of structural reform. From 2000 onwards, however, the Romanian economy was transformed into one

of relative <color=#3366CC>macroeconomic</color> stability, characterised by <color=#3366CC>high growth</color>, low <color=#3366CC>unemployment</color> and declining <color=#3366CC>inflation</color>. In 2006,
according to the Romanian Statistics Office, GDP growth in real terms was recorded at 7.7%, one of the highest rates
in <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>. However, the <color=#3366CC>Great Recession</color> forced the government to borrow externally, including an <color=#3366CC>IMF</color> €20 billion
bailout programme. According to <color=#3366CC>The World Bank</color>, GDP per capita in <color=#3366CC>purchasing power parity</color> grew from $13,703 in
Romania's main exports are <color=#3366CC>vehicles</color>, software, clothing and textiles, industrial machinery, electrical and <color=#3366CC>electronic</color>

<color=#3366CC>equipment</color>, <color=#3366CC>metallurgic products</color>, raw materials, <color=#3366CC>military equipment</color>, <color=#3366CC>pharmaceuticals</color>, fine chemicals, and <color=#3366CC>agricultural</color>

<color=#3366CC>products</color> (<color=#3366CC>fruits</color>, <color=#3366CC>vegetables</color>, and <color=#3366CC>flowers</color>). Trade is mostly centred on the member states of the <color=#3366CC>EU</color>, with <color=#3366CC>Germany</color>, <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>
and <color=#3366CC>France</color> being the country's single largest <color=#3366CC>trading partners</color>.
In 2005, the government replaced Romania's progressive tax system with a flat tax of 16% for both personal income
and corporate profit, among the lowest rates in the EU. The economy is based predominantly on <color=#3366CC>services</color>, which
account for 56.2% of the country's total GDP as of 2017, with industry and <color=#3366CC>agriculture</color> accounting for 30% and 4.4%
respectively. Approximately 25.8% of the Romanian workforce is employed in agriculture, one of the highest rates in
<color=#3366CC>Europe</color>.
Romania has attracted increasing amounts of foreign investment following the end of <color=#3366CC>communism</color>, with the stock of
foreign direct investment (FDI) in Romania rising to €83.8 billion in June 2019. Romania's FDI outward stock (an
external or foreign business either investing in or purchasing the stock of a local economy) amounted to $745 million in
December 2018, the lowest value among the 28 EU member states.
Since 1867 the official currency has been the Romanian leu ("lion"), which "was redenominated, with the exchange rate
set at 1 new leu = 10,000 old lei" in 2005 according to the National Bank of Romania. As it joined the EU in 2007,
Romania plans to adopt the <color=#3366CC>euro</color> in 2029.
Infrastructure
According to the Romania's National Institute of Statistics (INS), Romania's total road network was estimated in 2015 at
86080 km. The <color=#3366CC>World Bank</color> estimates the railway network at 22298 km of track, the fourth-largest railway network in
<color=#3366CC>Europe</color>. Romania's rail transport experienced a dramatic decline after 1989 and was estimated at 99 million passenger
journeys in 2004, but has experienced a recent (2013) revival due to infrastructure improvements and partial
privatisation of lines, accounting for 45% of all <color=#3366CC>passenger</color> and <color=#3366CC>freight</color> movements in the country. Bucharest Metro, the
only <color=#3366CC>underground</color> railway system, was opened in 1979 and measures 80.01 km with an average ridership in 2021 of
720,000 passengers during the workweek in the country. There are sixteen international commercial airports in service
today. Over 12.8 million passengers flew through Bucharest's Henri Coandă International Airport in 2017.
Romania is a net exporter of electrical energy and is 52nd worldwide in terms of consumption of electric energy.
Around a third of the produced energy comes from renewable sources, mostly as <color=#3366CC>hydroelectric power</color>. It has one of the
largest refining capacities in <color=#3366CC>Eastern Europe</color>, even though <color=#3366CC>oil</color> and <color=#3366CC>natural gas</color> production has been decreasing for more
than a decade. With one of the largest reserves of <color=#3366CC>crude oil</color> and shale gas in Europe it is among the most
energy-independent countries in the EU, and is looking to expand its <color=#3366CC>nuclear power plant</color> at Cernavodă further.
There were almost 18.3 million connections to the <color=#3366CC>Internet</color> in June 2014. According to Bloomberg, in 2013 Romania
ranked fifth in the world, and according to The Independent, it ranks number one in Europe at Internet speeds, with
<color=#3366CC>Timisoara</color> ranked among the highest in the world.
Tourism
Tourism is a significant contributor to the Romanian economy, generating around 5% of GDP. The number of tourists
has been rising steadily, reaching 9.33 million foreign tourists in 2016, according to the <color=#3366CC>Worldbank</color>. Tourism in Romania
attracted €400 million in investments in 2005. More than 60% of the foreign visitors in 2007 were from other EU
countries. The popular summer attractions of Mamaia and other Black Sea Resorts attracted 1.3 million tourists in
Among Romania's spa towns and <color=#3366CC>resorts</color> are Buzias, Băile Călacea, Moneasa, Băile Lipova, Călimănesti, Amara, and
Geoagiu-Băi. At the same time, seaside resorts such as Eforie, Mangalia, Saturn, Venus, Neptun, Olimp, and Mamaia
(sometimes also called the Romanian Riviera) are among the main tourist attractions during the <color=#3366CC>summer</color>. Most popular
<color=#3366CC>skiing resorts</color> are along the Valea Prahovei, Muntele Mic, Semenic, Straja and Poiana Brasov. Wine tourism is
represented by areas such as Recas, Silagiu, Odobesti, Drăgăsani, and Podgoria Aradului.
Castles, fortifications, or strongholds as well as preserved medieval Transylvanian cities or towns such as <color=#3366CC>Timisoara</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Cluj-Napoca</color>, Sibiu, <color=#3366CC>Brasov</color>, Alba Iulia, Baia Mare, Bistrita, Medias, Cisnădie, Sebes, or Sighisoara also attract a large
number of tourists. Bran Castle, near Brasov, is one of the most famous attractions in Romania, drawing hundreds of
thousands of tourists every year as it is often (falsely) advertised as being Dracula's Castle. Other attractions include
the Danube Delta or the Sculptural Ensemble of Constantin Brâncusi at Târgu Jiu.
Rural tourism, focusing on getting visitors acquainted with local <color=#3366CC>folklore</color> and <color=#3366CC>customs</color>, has become an important
alternative, and is targeted to promote such sites as Bran and its Dracula's Castle, the painted churches of northern
Moldavia, and the wooden churches of Maramures, or the villages with fortified churches in Transylvania. The Via
Transilvanica long-distance hiking and cycling <color=#3366CC>trail</color>, which crosses 10 counties in the <color=#3366CC>Transylvania</color>, <color=#3366CC>Banat</color> and Bukovina
regions of the country further promotes rural slow tourism.
In 2014, Romania had 32,500 companies active in the hotel and restaurant industry, with a total turnover of €2.6 billion.
More than 1.9 million foreign tourists visited Romania in 2014, 12% more than in 2013. According to the country's

National Statistics Institute, some 77% came from <color=#3366CC>Europe</color> (particularly from <color=#3366CC>Germany</color>, <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>, and <color=#3366CC>France</color>), 12% from
<color=#3366CC>Asia</color>, and less than 7% from <color=#3366CC>North America</color>.
Science and technology
Historically, Romanian researchers and inventors have made notable contributions to several fields. In the history of
flight, Traian Vuia built the first <color=#3366CC>aeroplane</color> to take off under its own power and Aurel Vlaicu built and flew some of the
earliest successful aircraft, while Henri Coandă discovered the <color=#3366CC>Coandă effect</color> of fluidics. Victor Babes discovered more
than 50 types of bacteria; biologist Nicolae Paulescu developed an extract of the pancreas and showed that it lowers
blood sugar in diabetic dogs, thus being significant in the history of <color=#3366CC>insulin</color>; while Emil Palade received the <color=#3366CC>Nobel Prize</color>
for his contributions to <color=#3366CC>cell biology</color>. Lazăr Edeleanu was the first chemist to synthesise <color=#3366CC>amphetamine</color>, and he also
invented the procedure of separating valuable petroleum components with selective solvents.
During the 1990s and 2000s, the development of research was hampered by several factors, including <color=#3366CC>corruption</color>, low
funding, and a considerable brain drain. In recent years, Romania has ranked the lowest or second-lowest in the EU by
<color=#3366CC>research and development</color> spending as a percentage of GDP, standing at roughly 0.5% in 2016 and 2017, substantially
below the EU average of just over 2%. The country joined the <color=#3366CC>European Space Agency</color> (ESA) in 2011, and <color=#3366CC>CERN</color> in
2016. In 2018, however, Romania lost its voting rights in the ESA due to a failure to pay €56.8 million in membership
contributions to the agency.
In the early 2010s, the situation for science in Romania was characterised as "rapidly improving" albeit from a low base.
In January 2011, Parliament passed a law that enforces "strict quality control on universities and introduces tough rules
for funding evaluation and peer review". Romania was ranked 49th in the Global Innovation Index in 2025.
The <color=#3366CC>nuclear physics</color> facility of the EU's proposed Extreme Light Infrastructure (ELI) <color=#3366CC>laser</color> will be built in Romania. In
early 2012, Romania launched its first satellite from the Centre Spatial Guyanais in French Guiana. Starting in
December 2014, Romania became a co-owner of the <color=#3366CC>International Space Station</color>.
Demographics
According to the 2021 Romanian census, Romania's population was 19,053,815. Like other countries in the region, its
population is expected to decline gradually as a result of sub-replacement fertility rates and negative net migration rate.
According to the 2021 Romanian census, Romanians made up 89.33% of the population, Hungarians 6.05% and the
<color=#3366CC>Roma</color> 3.44% of the population, but many ethnicities are not recorded, as they do not have <color=#3366CC>ID cards</color>. International
sources give higher figures for Roma than the official census. According to the <color=#3366CC>Council of Europe</color>, the Roma make up
8.32% of the population; this figure is difficult to verify due to the mobility of Roma and the reluctance of some of them
to disclose their ethnicity. Hungarians constitute a majority in the counties of Harghita and Covasna. Other minorities
include Ukrainians, Germans, Turks, Lipovans, Aromanians, Tatars, and Serbs. In 1930, there were 745,421 Germans
living in Romania, but only about 36,000 remained in the country to this day. As of 2009, there were also approximately
133,000 immigrants living in Romania, primarily from <color=#3366CC>Moldova</color> and <color=#3366CC>China</color>.
The total fertility rate (TFR) in 2018 was estimated at 1.36 children born per woman, which is below the replacement
rate of 2.1, and one of the lowest in the world; it remains considerably below the high of 5.82 children born per woman
in 1912. In 2014, 31.2% of births were to unmarried women. The birth rate (9.49, 2012) is much lower than the mortality
rate (11.84, 2012), resulting in a shrinking (0.26% per year, 2012) and aging population (median age: 41.6 years,
2018), one of the oldest populations in the world, with approximately 16.8% of total population aged 65 years and over.
The life expectancy in 2015 was estimated at 74.92 years (71.46 years male, 78.59 years female). The number of
Romanians and individuals with ancestors born in Romania living abroad is estimated at 12 million. After the <color=#3366CC>Romanian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Revolution of 1989</color>, a significant number of Romanians emigrated to other European countries, <color=#3366CC>North America</color> or
<color=#3366CC>Australia</color>. For example, in 1990, 96,919 Romanians permanently settled abroad.
Urbanisation
Although 54.0% of the population lived in <color=#3366CC>urban areas</color> in 2011, this percentage has been declining since 1996.
Counties with over 2/3 urban population are Hunedoara, Brasov and Constanta, while those with less than a third are
Dâmbovita (30.06%) and Giurgiu and Teleorman. Bucharest is the capital and the largest city in Romania, with a
population of over 1.7 million in 2021. Its larger urban zone has a population of almost 2.2 million, which are planned to
be included into a metropolitan area up to 20 times the area of the city proper.
Another 17 cities have a population of over 100,000, with Cluj-Napoca, Iasi, Constanta and Timisoara having more than
250,000 inhabitants, and Craiova, Brasov and Galati with over 200,000 inhabitants. Metropolitan areas have been
constituted for most of these cities.
Languages
The official language is Romanian, a <color=#3366CC>Romance language</color> (the most widely spoken of the Eastern Romance branch),
which presents a consistent degree of similarity to Aromanian, Megleno-Romanian, and Istro-Romanian, but shares
many features equally with the rest of the Western Romance languages, specifically <color=#3366CC>Italian</color>, <color=#3366CC>French</color>, <color=#3366CC>Spanish</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Portuguese</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Catalan</color>. The Romanian alphabet contains the same 26 letters of the standard Latin alphabet, as well
as five additional ones (namely ă, â, î, t, and s), totalling 31.
Romanian is spoken as a first language by 91.55% of the entire population, while <color=#3366CC>Hungarian</color> and Vlax Romani are
spoken by 6.28% and 1.20% of the population, respectively. There are also 40,861 native speakers of <color=#3366CC>Ukrainian</color>
(concentrated in some compact regions near the border, where they form local majorities), 17,101 native speakers of
<color=#3366CC>Turkish</color>, 15,943 native speakers of <color=#3366CC>German</color>, and 14,414 native speakers of <color=#3366CC>Russian</color> living in Romania.
According to the Constitution, local councils ensure linguistic rights to all minorities. In localities with ethnic minorities of
over 20%, that minority's language can be used in the public administration, justice system, and education. Foreign
citizens and stateless persons who live in Romania have access to justice and education in their own language. <color=#3366CC>English</color>
and <color=#3366CC>French</color> are the main foreign languages taught in schools. In 2010, the Organisation internationale de la
Francophonie identified 4,756,100 French speakers in the country. According to the 2012 Eurobarometer, English is
spoken by 31% of Romanians, French is spoken by 17%, and <color=#3366CC>Italian</color> and <color=#3366CC>German</color>, each by 7%.
Religion
Romania is a secular state and has no <color=#3366CC>state religion</color>. An overwhelming majority of the population identify themselves as
Christians. At the country's 2021 census, 73.60% of respondents identified as <color=#3366CC>Orthodox Christians</color>, with 73.42%
belonging to the Romanian Orthodox Church. Other denominations include Protestantism (6.22%), Roman Catholicism
(3.89%), and Greek Catholicism (0.61%). From the remaining population 128,291 people belong to other <color=#3366CC>Christian</color>
<color=#3366CC>denominations</color> or have another religion, which includes 58,347 Muslims (mostly of <color=#3366CC>Turkish</color> and <color=#3366CC>Tatar</color> ethnicity) and
2,708 Jewish (Jews once constituted 4% of the Romanian population—728,115 persons in the 1930 census).
Additionally, 71,430 people are <color=#3366CC>irreligious</color>, 57,229 are <color=#3366CC>atheist</color>, 25,485 are <color=#3366CC>agnostic</color>, and 2,658,165 people chose to not
declare their religion.
The Romanian Orthodox Church is an autocephalous <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodox Church</color> in full communion with other Orthodox
churches, with a Patriarch as its leader. It is the third-largest Eastern Orthodox Church in the world, and unlike other
Orthodox churches, it functions within a <color=#3366CC>Latin</color> culture and uses a <color=#3366CC>Romance</color> liturgical language. Its canonical jurisdiction
covers the territories of Romania and <color=#3366CC>Moldova</color>. Romania has the world's third-largest Eastern Orthodox population.
Education
Since the <color=#3366CC>Romanian revolution</color> of 1989, the Romanian educational system has been in a continuous process of reform
that has received mixed criticism. In 2004, some 4.4 million individuals were enrolled in <color=#3366CC>school</color>. Of these, 650,000 were

in <color=#3366CC>kindergarten</color> (three-six years), 3.11 million in <color=#3366CC>primary</color> and <color=#3366CC>secondary</color> level, and 650,000 in tertiary level (<color=#3366CC>universities</color>).
In 2018, the adult <color=#3366CC>literacy rate</color> was 98.8%. Kindergarten is optional between three and five years. Since 2020,
<color=#3366CC>compulsory schooling</color> starts at age 5 with the last year of kindergarten (grupa mare) and is compulsory until twelfth
grade. Primary and secondary education is divided into 12 or 13 grades. There is also a semi-legal, informal <color=#3366CC>private</color>
<color=#3366CC>tutoring</color> system used mostly during secondary school, which prospered during the Communist regime.
As of 2025, Babes-Bolyai University of <color=#3366CC>Cluj-Napoca</color> and the University of Bucharest are included in the QS World
University Rankings' top 800.
Romania ranks fifth in the all-time medal count at the International Mathematical Olympiad with 316 total medals, dating
back to 1959. Ciprian Manolescu managed to write a perfect paper (42 points) for a gold medal more times than
anybody else in the history of the competition, in 1995, 1996 and 1997. Romania has achieved the highest team score

in the competition, after <color=#3366CC>China</color>, <color=#3366CC>Russia</color>, the <color=#3366CC>United States</color> and <color=#3366CC>Hungary</color>. Romania also ranks sixth in the all-time medal
count at the International Olympiad in Informatics with 107 total medals, dating back to 1989.
Health
Healthcare in Romania is mainly provided by the public sector, which runs most hospitals and offers national health
insurance to nearly all citizens. In 2021, healthcare costs were US$16. 7 billion, or US$2,385 per person, making up
€5.69 of GDP. Government spending is higher than in markets like <color=#3366CC>Bulgaria</color> but lower than <color=#3366CC>Hungary</color>. Spending is
expected to rise by 7. US$5 billion (+37. 68%) from 2024 to 2028, reaching 27. US$3 billion by 2028.
The Romanian National Institute of Statistics reports over 65,000 health units in Romania, with 53,000 in <color=#3366CC>urban areas</color>
and 12,000 in <color=#3366CC>rural areas</color>. There are 543 <color=#3366CC>hospitals</color>, including 488 in urban and 55 in rural areas, along with 160 other
hospital-like establishments. Nearly 50% of these are large facilities with over 100 beds, while 39% are small with fewer
than 50 beds. The total number of inpatient beds is 135,085, allocated mainly to <color=#3366CC>psychiatry</color>, <color=#3366CC>surgery</color>, and <color=#3366CC>internal</color>
<color=#3366CC>medicine</color> among other specialties.
Culture
Holidays and traditions
There are 12 non-working public holidays, including the Great Union Day, celebrated on 1 December in
commemoration of the 1918 union of <color=#3366CC>Transylvania</color> with Romania. Winter holidays include the <color=#3366CC>Christmas</color> and <color=#3366CC>New Year</color>
festivities during which various unique <color=#3366CC>folklore dances</color> and <color=#3366CC>games</color> are common: plugusorul, sorcova, ursul, and capra.
The traditional Romanian dress that otherwise has largely fallen out of use during the 20th century, is a popular
ceremonial vestment worn on these <color=#3366CC>festivities</color>, especially in <color=#3366CC>rural areas</color>. There are sacrifices of live <color=#3366CC>pigs</color> during
Christmas and lambs during <color=#3366CC>Easter</color> that has required a special exemption from <color=#3366CC>EU</color> law after 2007. In the Easter,
traditions such as <color=#3366CC>painting the eggs</color> are very common. On 1 March mărtisor gifting is featured, which is a <color=#3366CC>tradition</color>
whereby females are gifted with a type of talisman that is given for <color=#3366CC>good luck</color>.
Arts and monuments
Architecture
The topic of the origin of Romanian culture began to be discussed by the end of the 18th century among the
Transylvanian School scholars. Several writers rose to prominence in the 19th century, including: George Cosbuc, Ioan
Slavici, Mihail Kogălniceanu, Vasile Alecsandri, Nicolae Bălcescu, <color=#3366CC>Ion Luca Caragiale</color>, Ion Creangă, and <color=#3366CC>Mihai</color>
<color=#3366CC>Eminescu</color>, the later being considered the greatest and most influential Romanian poet, particularly for the poem
Luceafărul.
In the 20th century, a number of Romanian artists and writers achieved international acclaim, including: <color=#3366CC>Tristan Tzara</color>,
Marcel Janco, <color=#3366CC>Mircea Eliade</color>, Nicolae Grigorescu, Marin Preda, Liviu Rebreanu, <color=#3366CC>Eugène Ionesco</color>, <color=#3366CC>Emil Cioran</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>Constantin Brâncusi</color>. Brâncusi has a sculptural ensemble in Târgu Jiu, while his sculpture <color=#3366CC>Bird in Space</color>, was auctioned
in 2005 for $27.5 million. Romanian-born <color=#3366CC>Holocaust</color> survivor <color=#3366CC>Elie Wiesel</color> received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1986, while
Banat Swabian writer <color=#3366CC>Herta Müller</color> received the 2009 Nobel Prize in Literature.
Prominent Romanian painters include: Nicolae Grigorescu, Stefan Luchian, Ion Andreescu Nicolae Tonitza, and
Theodor Aman. Notable Romanian classical composers of the 19th and 20th centuries include: Ciprian Porumbescu,
Anton Pann, Eduard Caudella, Mihail Jora, <color=#3366CC>Dinu Lipatti</color>, and especially <color=#3366CC>George Enescu</color>. The annual George Enescu
Festival is held in Bucharest in honour of the 20th-century composer.
Contemporary musicians like Angela Gheorghiu, <color=#3366CC>Gheorghe Zamfir</color>, Inna, Alexandra Stan, and many others have
achieved various levels of international acclaim. From the late 2000s through the early 2010s, the Romanian popcorn
music style had established itself in the international mainstream. At the <color=#3366CC>Eurovision Song Contest</color> Romanian singers
achieved third place in 2005 and 2010.
In cinema, several movies of the Romanian New Wave have achieved international acclaim. At the <color=#3366CC>Cannes Film</color>
<color=#3366CC>Festival</color>, The Death of Mr. Lazarescu by Cristi Puiu won the Prix Un Certain Regard in 2005, while 4 Months, 3 Weeks
and 2 Days by Cristian Mungiu won the festival's top prize, the Palme d'Or, in 2007. At the Berlin International Film
Festival, Child's Pose by Călin Peter Netzer won the Golden Bear in 2013.
The list of <color=#3366CC>World Heritage Sites</color> includes six cultural sites located within Romania, including eight painted churches of
northern Moldavia, eight wooden churches of Maramures, seven villages with fortified churches in <color=#3366CC>Transylvania</color>, the
Horezu Monastery, and the Historic Centre of Sighisoara. The city of Sibiu, with its Brukenthal National Museum, was
selected as the 2007 European Capital of Culture and the 2019 European Region of Gastronomy. Multiple castles exist
in Romania, including the popular tourist attractions of Peles Castle, Corvin Castle, and Bran Castle or "Dracula's
Castle".
Media
Cuisine
Romanian cuisine has been influenced by Austrian and <color=#3366CC>German cuisine</color> (especially in the historical regions that had
been formerly administered by the <color=#3366CC>Habsburg monarchy</color>), but also shares some similarities with other cuisines in the
<color=#3366CC>Balkan region</color> such as <color=#3366CC>Greek</color>, Bulgarian, and Serbian cuisine. Ciorbă includes a wide range of sour soups, while mititei,
mămăligă (similar to polenta), and sarmale are featured commonly in <color=#3366CC>main courses</color>.

<color=#3366CC>Pork</color>, <color=#3366CC>chicken</color>, and <color=#3366CC>beef</color> are the preferred types of <color=#3366CC>meat</color>, but <color=#3366CC>lamb</color> and <color=#3366CC>fish</color> are also quite popular. Certain traditional
recipes are made in direct connection with the <color=#3366CC>holidays</color>: chiftele, tobă and tochitură at Christmas; drob, pască and
cozonac at Easter and other Romanian holidays. Tuică is a strong plum <color=#3366CC>brandy</color> reaching a 70% alcohol content which
is the country's traditional <color=#3366CC>alcoholic beverage</color>, taking as much as 75% of the national crop (Romania is one of the
largest plum producers in the world). Traditional alcoholic beverages also include wine, rachiu, palincă and visinată, but
beer consumption has increased dramatically over recent years. In 2019, Romania became the country with the highest
alcohol consumption per capita.
Sports
<color=#3366CC>Football</color> is the most popular sport in Romania with over 219,000 registered players as of 2018. The market for
professional football in Romania was roughly €740 million in 2018 according to <color=#3366CC>UEFA</color>.
The governing body is the Romanian Football Federation, which belongs to UEFA. The Romania national football team
played its first match in 1922 and is one of only four national teams to have taken part in the first three <color=#3366CC>FIFA World</color>

<color=#3366CC>Cups</color>, the other three being <color=#3366CC>Brazil</color>, <color=#3366CC>France</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Belgium</color>. Overall, it has played in seven World Cups and had its most
successful period during the 1990s, when it finished 6th at the 1994 FIFA World Cup, eventually being ranked 3rd by
<color=#3366CC>FIFA</color> in 1997.
The most successful club is Steaua Bucuresti, who were the first Eastern European team to win the <color=#3366CC>UEFA Champions</color>
<color=#3366CC>League</color> in 1986, and were runners-up in 1989. Dinamo Bucuresti reached the UEFA Champions League semi-final in
1984 and the UEFA Cup Winners' Cup semi-final in 1990. Other important Romanian football clubs are Rapid
Bucuresti, UTA Arad, Universitatea Craiova, Petrolul Ploiesti, CFR Cluj, Astra Giurgiu, and Viitorul Constanta (the latter
having recently merged with FCV Farul Constanta).
Tennis is the second most popular sport. Romania reached the Davis Cup finals three times in 1969, 1971 and 1972.
The second most popular team sport is <color=#3366CC>handball</color>. The men's team won the handball world championship in 1961, 1964,
1970, 1974 making them the third most successful nation ever in the tournament. The women's team won the world
championship in 1962 and have enjoyed more success than their male counterparts in recent years. In the club
competition Romanian teams have won the EHF Champions League a total of three times, Steaua Bucuresti won in
1968 as well as 1977 and Dinamo Bucuresti won in 1965. In women's handball, powerhouse CSM Bucuresti lifted the
EHF Champions League trophy in 2016.
Popular individual sports include combat sports, martial arts, and swimming. In professional boxing, Romania has
produced many world champions across the weight divisions internationally recognised by governing bodies. Another
popular combat sport is <color=#3366CC>professional kickboxing</color>, which has produced prominent practitioners including.
Romania's 306 all-time Summer Olympics medals would rank 12th most among all countries, while its 89 gold medals
would be 14th most. The 1984 Summer Olympics was their most successful run, where they won 53 medals in total, 20
of them gold, ultimately placing 2nd to the hosts <color=#3366CC>United States</color> in the medal rankings. Amongst countries who have
never hosted the event themselves, they are second in the total number of medals earned. <color=#3366CC>Gymnastics</color> is the country's
major medal-producing sport.
